pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 130: Growing: nothing visible. (That's the point.)*

It snowed on a Wednesday. Not the grey, dusty flakes we get in London, but real, white, heavy snow that landed on the car park and turned the concrete the color of old milk. For one day, Lowell Court looked like a place where things might actually grow. The bins were white caps. The broken pigeon feeder wore a hat. Even the rail cutting looked soft.

I went to the garden. The outdoor beds were blank slates, buried under a quiet, white silence. I pulled my collar up and walked past the Spring Room, past the Summer Room where the wilting plants were tucked under frost cloth. At the back, behind the last hedge door, which was stuck tight with ice, I found the glass.

It was a small house, all panes and iron frames, dark inside. I pushed the door open. The air rushed out, warm and thick, smelling of wet earth and cold clay. Inside, rows of clay pots sat in neat lines. There were a hundred of them. Two hundred. I lost count. And in every single one, there was nothing. Just dark soil, waiting.
pages.image: Sana, thin with brown skin and round glasses, stands before a dark glass greenhouse in a snowy concrete estate, pushing the door open to release warm earthy air, with snow falling on the grey blocks behind her.

pages.text:
Gherkin was on his usual log, which meant he was about to be unhelpful. He looked pleased, and a tortoise looking pleased is a specific kind of danger that usually precedes a lecture.

"This," he said, his voice heavy in the warm glass air, "is the most important room."

I looked at the rows of empty pots. "It’s empty."

"It is full of waiting," Gherkin corrected. He blinked one eye slowly. "Every seed here has been planted. Nothing shows. You cannot see them. You cannot measure them. You must believe they are there, even when you cannot prove it."

I crossed my arms over my chest. The glass reflected my face back at me, round glasses and all, making me look like a very serious librarian. "That sounds dreadful. It’s just... dirt."

"Mm," said Gherkin. He took a long, slow bite of lettuce, chewing with the distinct rhythm of someone who has never once been in a hurry. "Yes. That is the point, Sana. It is dirt. And it is alive. And you cannot rush it. Not here. Not ever."
pages.image: Gherkin, an old mossy tortoise the size of a hat, sits on a wooden log inside a glass greenhouse, chewing a lettuce leaf, with Sana standing nearby with her arms crossed, looking skeptical.

pages.text:
The Winter Room ran on a different set of rules. There was no audience to perform for, and no one to show off to. I planted the seed, spoke my true thing, and then I simply waited. Water in the morning, water at dusk. Do nothing else until spring. I might never actually see it grow.

I pulled a small brown seed from my pocket. It was a poppy, tiny and rough like a single grain of coarse sand. I dug a shallow hole in the dark soil of the clay pot, dropped the seed in, and covered it up.

I closed my eyes. I did not say the true thing out loud, because out loud it felt too big and might break. Instead, I said it only inside my head, where it was safe and small and didn’t need to be perfect. I could feel Gherkin’s eyes on me, heavy and warm like a cat sleeping on a notebook. He did not speak. He did not ask. He just watched me cover the seed with my thumb, pressing the soil down, down, down, until my thumb was red and the seed was gone.
pages.image: A close-up of Sana’s hand, wearing a patched denim sleeve, pressing a small brown seed into dark soil in a clay pot, with the mossy shell of a tortoise visible in the background.

pages.text:
Day one, I watered. Day two, I watered. Day three, I watered. Nothing happened, which was exactly what the rules said should happen, so that was good.

On day four, I stood over the pot and my hand started to twitch. I reached in with one finger, just to poke the soil, just to see if it had moved or if it was even there anymore. I didn’t want to dig, not really. I just wanted to check.

My finger hit the cold earth. I froze.

I pulled my hand back and shoved it into my pocket, where my heart was beating fast and loud, like a drum in a small room. I walked out of the glass house and went to find Theo, who was mending the fence with a roll of wire. I didn’t tell him I’d almost broken the rule. I just handed him the wire cutter and helped him twist the metal. I had beaten myself, and it was the first time.
pages.image: Sana and Theo, a boy in a beanie and hoodie, stand in the snowy garden mending a chain-link fence with wire, Sana holding a wire cutter, looking focused and quiet.

pages.text:
I sat on the bench outside the Winter Room, watching snow settle on the glass. Above me, from the window of Block C, a red scarf hung over the railing. It was so long it almost touched the pavement.

Mrs. Ilves was leaning over her window, knitting. The needle clicked, and the yarn pulled, and the scarf grew.

"Four meters," she called down. Her voice was thin in the cold air. "I started it the day the garden was shut. Thirty years ago. One row a day."

I looked at the red wool, stretching across the grey concrete, a bright line against the white snow. "Who is it for?" I asked.

She didn’t answer. She just pulled the yarn through, adding another row to the long, red wait. I went back inside, checked the pot, and watered it.
pages.image: A long red knitted scarf hangs over the concrete railing of an apartment block, stretching down toward the snow-covered garden below, with a small glass greenhouse visible in the distance.
